name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q01 - Structure of stamen, anther, and microsporangium

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements regarding the male reproductive structure in angiosperms and choose the correct option:

Statement I: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed and dithecous, consisting of four microsporangia located at the corners.

Statement II: The outer three wall layers of a microsporangium (epidermis, endothecium, and middle layers) perform the function of protection and help in the dehiscence of the anther.

Statement III: Cells of the tapetum possess sparse cytoplasm and are strictly uninucleate throughout pollen development.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In flowering plants, the stamen consists of a filament and a terminal anther. The internal organisation of the anther includes four microsporangia surrounded by four distinct wall layers with specialised roles in protection, dehiscence, and nutrition.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Anther Structure
A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed, and each lobe has two thecae (dithecous). In a transverse section, it appears as a four-sided (tetragonal) structure with four microsporangia located at the four corners, two in each lobe. Thus, the description of the anther as bilobed, dithecous, and tetrasporangiate is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Microsporangium Wall Layers
A microsporangium is surrounded by four wall layers: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, and tapetum. The outer three layers (epidermis, endothecium, and middle layers) protect the developing microspores and assist in anther dehiscence to release pollen grains. Thus, the role attributed to the outer three wall layers is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Tapetum
The innermost wall layer is the tapetum, which nourishes the developing pollen grains. Contrary to having sparse cytoplasm and being strictly uninucleate, tapetal cells possess dense cytoplasm and generally contain more than one nucleus. Therefore, the claim that tapetal cells have sparse cytoplasm and are strictly uninucleate is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Only the first two claims regarding the bilobed dithecous anther and the protective/dehiscence role of the outer three wall layers are correct, whereas the claim regarding the tapetum is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q02 - Pollen grain wall layers and cellular stages

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements about angiosperm pollen grains and select the correct option:

Statement I: The exine is composed of sporopollenin, which is absent at prominent apertures called germ pores.

Statement II: The intine is a thick, discontinuous outer layer made up of cellulose and lignin.

Statement III: In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at the 2-celled stage containing a vegetative cell and a generative cell.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollen grains represent the male gametophytes in angiosperms and possess a specialised two-layered wall (sporoderm) along with either two or three cells at the time of shedding.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Exine and Germ Pores
The hard outer wall layer, the exine, is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known, capable of withstanding high temperatures, strong acids, and alkalis. At specific apertures called germ pores, sporopollenin is absent so that the pollen tube can emerge during germination. Therefore, the claim about the exine and germ pores is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Intine
The inner wall of the pollen grain is the intine. It is a thin and continuous layer composed of cellulose and pectin, not a thick, discontinuous outer layer made of cellulose and lignin. Therefore, the claim describing the intine is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Pollen Shedding Stage
At maturity, a pollen grain contains a larger vegetative cell with abundant food reserves and a smaller, spindle-shaped generative cell floating in its cytoplasm. In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at this 2-celled stage, while in the remaining species the generative cell divides mitotically before shedding to form a 3-celled stage. Therefore, the claim about shedding at the 2-celled stage is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the sporopollenin exine with germ pores and the 2-celled shedding stage in over 60 per cent of angiosperms are correct, while the description of the intine is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q03 - Pollen allergy, nutrition, and cryopreservation viability

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding pollen grains and their economic and biological significance:

Statement I: Parthenium (carrot grass) entered India as a contaminant with imported wheat and causes severe pollen allergy.

Statement II: Pollen grains of rice and wheat retain viability for several months after release.

Statement III: Pollen grains of a large number of species can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\) for use in pollen banks.

How many of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollen grains vary in their allergenic potential, nutritional richness, and duration of viability after shedding, and they can be cryopreserved for crop breeding programmes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Parthenium and Pollen Allergy
Parthenium, commonly known as carrot grass, came into India as a contaminant with imported wheat, became ubiquitous, and causes severe pollen allergies and chronic respiratory disorders such as asthma and bronchitis. Thus, the claim about Parthenium is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Pollen Viability in Cereals
Pollen viability depends on prevailing temperature and humidity and varies widely across taxa. In cereals such as rice and wheat, pollen grains lose viability within 30 minutes of their release, whereas members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae maintain viability for months. Thus, the claim that rice and wheat pollen remain viable for months is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Pollen Storage in Liquid Nitrogen
Pollen grains of many species can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\) and used as pollen banks, similar to seed banks, in crop breeding programmes. Thus, the claim about cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Exactly two of the three claims—those concerning Parthenium pollen allergy and long-term storage in liquid nitrogen—are correct, while the claim regarding cereal pollen viability is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q04 - Gynoecium types and structure of anatropous ovule

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements regarding the female reproductive part of a flower and choose the correct option:

Statement I: The gynoecium of Papaver is multicarpellary and syncarpous, whereas that of Michelia is multicarpellary and apocarpous.

Statement II: The hilum represents the junction between the body of the ovule and the funicle.

Statement III: The chalaza represents the small opening at the tip of the integuments where the pollen tube enters the ovule.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The gynoecium may consist of one or more pistils that are either fused (syncarpous) or free (apocarpous). Inside the ovary, ovules (megasporangia) are attached to the placenta and possess characteristic anatomical regions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Syncarpous and Apocarpous Gynoecium
In Papaver, multiple pistils are fused together, forming a multicarpellary syncarpous pistil. In contrast, Michelia has multiple free pistils, representing a multicarpellary apocarpous gynoecium. Therefore, the comparison between Papaver and Michelia is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Hilum and Funicle
An ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the funicle, and the body of the ovule fuses with the funicle at a region called the hilum. Hence, the hilum indeed represents the junction between the ovule and the funicle.

Step 4: Evaluation of Chalaza and Micropyle
Protective envelopes called integuments encircle the nucellus except at a small opening at the tip called the micropyle. Opposite to the micropylar end lies the chalaza, which represents the basal part of the ovule. Describing the chalaza as the small opening at the tip of the integuments is therefore incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the gynoecium of Papaver and Michelia and the role of the hilum are correct, whereas the claim defining the chalaza as the micropylar opening is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q05 - Megasporogenesis and monosporic embryo sac development

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding megasporogenesis and female gametophyte development in angiosperms:

Statement I: A single megaspore mother cell differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus and undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid megaspores.

Statement II: The mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore nucleus to form the 8-nucleate stage are strictly free-nuclear.

Statement III: At maturity, a typical angiosperm embryo sac is 7-celled and 8-nucleate, with the filiform apparatus located in the antipodal cells at the chalazal end.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Megasporogenesis produces haploid megaspores from a diploid megaspore mother cell (MMC), and in most angiosperms a single functional megaspore undergoes monosporic development to form the mature female gametophyte (embryo sac).

Step 2: Evaluation of Megasporogenesis
Ovules generally differentiate a single large MMC with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus in the micropylar region of the nucellus. The MMC undergoes meiotic division to produce four haploid megaspores. Thus, the description of MMC differentiation and meiosis is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Free-Nuclear Mitotic Divisions
In monosporic development, one megaspore remains functional while the other three degenerate. The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to form 2-nucleate, 4-nucleate, and 8-nucleate stages. These mitotic divisions are strictly free-nuclear—that is, nuclear divisions are not immediately followed by cell wall formation—until after the 8-nucleate stage. Thus, the claim about free-nuclear divisions is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Mature Embryo Sac Organisation
After cell wall formation, six of the eight nuclei become organised into cells and two polar nuclei remain in the large central cell, making the mature embryo sac 7-celled and 8-nucleate. However, the filiform apparatus consists of special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip of the two synergids (part of the egg apparatus) to guide the pollen tube, not in the antipodal cells at the chalazal end. Thus, the location of the filiform apparatus is stated incorrectly.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding MMC meiosis and free-nuclear mitotic divisions are correct, whereas the claim placing the filiform apparatus in the antipodals is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q06 - Autogamy, cleistogamy, geitonogamy, and xenogamy

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding types of pollination in flowering plants:

Statement I: Cleistogamous flowers in plants such as Viola, Oxalis, and Commelina do not open at all and are invariably autogamous, ensuring seed-set even without pollinators.

Statement II: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination involving a pollinating agent, but genetically it is similar to autogamy.

Statement III: Xenogamy transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower on the same plant, bringing genetically identical pollen to the stigma.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on the source of pollen, pollination is classified into autogamy (same flower), geitonogamy (different flower, same plant), and xenogamy (different plant), each having distinct ecological and genetic consequences.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cleistogamous Flowers
Plants such as Viola (common pansy), Oxalis, and Commelina produce both chasmogamous (open) and cleistogamous (closed) flowers. Because cleistogamous flowers never open and their anthers and stigma lie close together, cross-pollen cannot land on the stigma. Hence, they are invariably autogamous and produce assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.

Step 3: Evaluation of Geitonogamy
Geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of another flower of the same plant. Functionally it requires a pollinating agent (like cross-pollination), but because the pollen comes from the same plant, it is genetically similar to autogamy.

Step 4: Evaluation of Xenogamy
Xenogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a different plant. It is the only type of pollination that brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma. Describing xenogamy as transfer between flowers of the same plant with genetically identical pollen is therefore incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding cleistogamous flowers and geitonogamy are correct, whereas the claim defining xenogamy is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q07 - Wind and water pollination adaptations in angiosperms

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements regarding abiotic pollination in flowering plants:

Statement I: Wind-pollinated flowers generally have light, non-sticky pollen grains, well-exposed stamens, and large feathery stigmas, and they often contain a single ovule in each ovary.

Statement II: All aquatic plants, including water hyacinth and water lily, use water currents as their agent of pollination.

Statement III: In marine seagrasses like Zostera, female flowers remain submerged and pollen grains are long, ribbon-like, and protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abiotic pollination uses wind or water and relies on chance contact between pollen and stigma, leading to specific floral and pollen adaptations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Wind Pollination
Wind pollination is the more common abiotic mode and is widespread in grasses. Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, non-sticky pollen, possess well-exposed stamens for easy dispersal, have large feathery stigmas to trap air-borne pollen, and often bear a single ovule in each ovary with numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence (such as the tassels of a corn cob). This description is completely accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of Aquatic Plant Pollination
Pollination by water (hydrophily) is quite rare in flowering plants, limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons (such as Vallisneria, Hydrilla, and Zostera). In a majority of aquatic plants, such as water hyacinth and water lily, the flowers emerge above the water level and are pollinated by insects or wind rather than water. Hence, claiming that all aquatic plants use water for pollination is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Submerged Hydrophily in Seagrasses
In seagrasses like Zostera, female flowers remain submerged and pollen grains are released inside the water. These pollen grains are long and ribbon-like, carried passively by water, and protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering. This description is accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding wind-pollinated floral adaptations and submerged pollination in seagrasses are correct, whereas the claim that all aquatic plants are water-pollinated is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q08 - Biotic pollination, floral rewards, and mutualism

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding animal-mediated pollination:

Statement I: Flowers pollinated by flies and beetles often secrete foul odours to attract these animals.

Statement II: In Yucca, a moth species deposits its eggs in the locule of the ovary and pollinates the flower in return, so neither organism can complete its life cycle without the other.

Statement III: All insects that visit flowers to consume nectar or pollen necessarily bring about pollination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Majority of flowering plants rely on biotic agents (such as bees, flies, beetles, moths, birds, and bats) and offer floral rewards like nectar, pollen, or safe egg-laying sites to sustain visits.

Step 2: Evaluation of Fly and Beetle Pollination
Animals are attracted by colour and/or fragrance. Specifically, flowers pollinated by flies and beetles secrete foul odours to attract these pollinators. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Yucca–Moth Relationship
In some species, floral rewards consist of providing safe places to lay eggs (as in Amorphophallus and Yucca). In Yucca, the moth deposits its eggs in the ovarian locule while pollinating the flower, and the larvae emerge as the seeds start developing; neither species can complete its life cycle without the other. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Pollen and Nectar Robbers
Only floral visitors that come into contact with both the anthers and the stigma can bring about pollination. Many insects consume pollen or nectar without touching the reproductive structures and therefore do not effect pollination; such visitors are known as pollen/nectar robbers. Hence, claiming that all nectar- or pollen-consuming visitors bring about pollination is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims about foul-odour attraction in fly/beetle-pollinated flowers and the obligate mutualism between Yucca and its moth are correct, while the claim that all floral visitors pollinate is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q09 - Outbreeding devices and prevention of self-pollination

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding outbreeding devices in flowering plants:

Statement I: Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.

Statement II: Production of unisexual flowers on the same plant (monoecious condition, as in castor and maize) prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.

Statement III: Dioecy (male and female flowers on different plants, as in papaya) prevents geitonogamy but cannot prevent autogamy.

How many of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Continued self-pollination leads to inbreeding depression, so flowering plants have evolved outbreeding devices such as dichogamy, herkogamy, self-incompatibility, monoecy, and dioecy to discourage self-pollination.

Step 2: Evaluation of Self-Incompatibility
Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (either from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination on the stigma or pollen tube growth in the pistil. This description is accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of Monoecious Plants
In monoecious plants like castor and maize, separate male and female flowers are borne on the same plant. Because a single flower lacks both sexes, autogamy is prevented, but pollen from a male flower can still reach a female flower on the same plant, so geitonogamy is not prevented. This description is accurate.

Step 4: Evaluation of Dioecious Plants
In dioecious plants like papaya, each individual plant is either male or female. Because male and female flowers are on separate plants, neither autogamy (same flower) nor geitonogamy (different flower on the same plant) can occur. Claiming that dioecy cannot prevent autogamy is therefore incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Exactly two of the three claims—those explaining self-incompatibility and monoecy in castor and maize—are correct, while the claim regarding dioecy failing to prevent autogamy is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q10 - Pollen-pistil interaction and artificial hybridisation

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements about pollen-pistil interaction and artificial hybridisation:

Statement I: The recognition and acceptance or rejection of pollen by the pistil is mediated by a continuous chemical dialogue between components of the pollen and the pistil.

Statement II: In plants where pollen is shed at the 2-celled condition, the generative cell divides to form two male gametes during the growth of the pollen tube in the stigma.

Statement III: Emasculation is essential even when the female parent produces unisexual female flowers.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollen-pistil interaction encompasses all events from pollen deposition on the stigma until the pollen tube enters the ovule, and artificial hybridisation uses emasculation and bagging to control pollination.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pollen Recognition
The pistil recognises whether landed pollen is compatible or incompatible through a continuous dialogue mediated by chemical components of the pollen interacting with those of the pistil, leading to promotion or inhibition of pollen germination and tube growth. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Male Gamete Formation in 2-Celled Pollen
When pollen grains are shed at the 2-celled stage (one vegetative cell and one generative cell), the generative cell divides mitotically to produce the two male gametes during the growth of the pollen tube in the stigma. In contrast, 3-celled pollen tubes carry two male gametes from the beginning. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Emasculation in Unisexual Flowers
Emasculation—the removal of anthers from a flower bud before dehiscence—is required only when the female parent bears bisexual flowers. If the female parent produces unisexual flowers, there are no anthers on the female flower, so emasculation is not needed; the female flower buds are simply bagged before opening. Claiming emasculation is essential for unisexual female flowers is therefore incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding chemical-mediated pollen-pistil dialogue and division of the generative cell in 2-celled pollen are correct, whereas the claim requiring emasculation in unisexual female flowers is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q11 - Double fertilisation, syngamy, and triple fusion

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding double fertilisation in flowering plants:

Statement I: The pollen tube discharges two male gametes into the cytoplasm of one of the synergids.

Statement II: Syngamy involves the fusion of one male gamete with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote.

Statement III: Triple fusion involves the fusion of the other male gamete with two polar nuclei in the central cell to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Double fertilisation is an event unique to flowering plants (angiosperms) in which two distinct fusion events—syngamy and triple fusion—occur within a single embryo sac.

Step 2: Evaluation of Gamete Discharge
After entering one of the synergids through the filiform apparatus, the pollen tube releases both male gametes into the cytoplasm of that synergid. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Syngamy
One of the two haploid male gametes moves towards the haploid egg cell and fuses with its nucleus. This fusion is called syngamy and produces a diploid cell, the zygote, which later develops into the embryo. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Triple Fusion
The second haploid male gamete moves towards the two haploid polar nuclei located in the large central cell and fuses with them. Because three haploid nuclei fuse together, this is called triple fusion and results in a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) inside the primary endosperm cell (PEC). Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three claims accurately describe the sequence and products of double fertilisation in angiosperms.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q12 - Endosperm development and albuminous versus non-albuminous seeds

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding endosperm development in angiosperms:

Statement I: Endosperm development precedes embryo development as an adaptation to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo.

Statement II: In tender coconut, the coconut water represents cellular endosperm, whereas the surrounding white kernel represents free-nuclear endosperm.

Statement III: Endosperm is completely consumed during embryo development in pea and groundnut, whereas it persists in mature seeds of castor and coconut.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Following triple fusion, the primary endosperm cell divides repeatedly to form nutritive triploid endosperm tissue, which supports the developing embryo and may or may not persist in the mature seed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Timing of Endosperm Development
Most zygotes divide only after a certain amount of endosperm is formed. Endosperm development precedes embryo development specifically to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Coconut Endosperm
In the common free-nuclear type of endosperm development, the PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to produce free nuclei before cell walls form. In tender coconut, the coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm (made of thousands of nuclei), while the surrounding white kernel is the cellular endosperm. Reversing these two forms makes the second claim incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Persistence of Endosperm
In non-albuminous (ex-albuminous) seeds such as pea, groundnut, and beans, the endosperm is completely consumed by the developing embryo before seed maturation. In albuminous seeds such as castor, coconut, wheat, maize, and barley, the endosperm persists in the mature seed and is used during germination. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding endosperm preceding embryo development and the examples of consumed versus persistent endosperm are correct, whereas the claim reversing free-nuclear and cellular endosperm in coconut is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q13 - Structure of dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous embryos

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements regarding embryo structure in dicotyledons and monocotyledons:

Statement I: In a typical dicot embryo, the portion of the embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule.

Statement II: In the grass family, the single lateral cotyledon is called the scutellum.

Statement III: In a monocot embryo, the coleorrhiza encloses the shoot apex and leaf primordia, while the coleoptile encloses the radicle and root cap.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although early embryogeny (proembryo, globular, and heart-shaped stages) is similar, mature dicot and monocot embryos differ in cotyledon number and protective sheaths.

Step 2: Evaluation of Dicot Embryo Axis
A typical dicotyledonous embryo has an embryonal axis and two cotyledons. The portion above the cotyledons is the epicotyl, ending in the plumule (stem tip), while the cylindrical portion below the cotyledons is the hypocotyl, ending in the radicle (root tip) covered by a root cap. Thus, the description of the epicotyl and plumule is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Scutellum
Monocotyledonous embryos possess a single cotyledon. In the grass family, this cotyledon is called the scutellum and is situated laterally on one side of the embryonal axis. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Coleoptile and Coleorrhiza
At the lower end of the grass embryonal axis, the radicle and root cap are enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called the coleorrhiza. Above the attachment of the scutellum, the epicotyl has a shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure called the coleoptile. Reversing coleorrhiza and coleoptile makes the third claim incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the dicot epicotyl and the grass scutellum are correct, whereas the claim swapping the functions of coleorrhiza and coleoptile is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q14 - Perisperm, false fruits, parthenocarpy, and seed longevity

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding seeds and fruits in angiosperms:

Statement I: In seeds of black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus persist and are referred to as perisperm.

Statement II: In apple, strawberry, and cashew, the thalamus contributes to fruit formation, so they are called false fruits.

Statement III: Parthenocarpic fruits such as banana develop without fertilisation and normally contain numerous viable seeds.

How many of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As ovules mature into seeds and ovaries develop into fruits, different floral and ovular tissues can persist or contribute to fruit structure, while some fruits form without fertilisation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Perisperm
Occasionally, in seeds such as black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus are not completely used up and remain persistent. This residual, persistent nucellus is called the perisperm. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of False Fruits
While most fruits develop solely from the ovary (true fruits), in a few species such as apple, strawberry, and cashew, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation. Such fruits are termed false fruits. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Parthenocarpic Fruits
In a few species such as banana, fruits develop without fertilisation and are called parthenocarpic fruits. Parthenocarpy can also be induced using growth hormones, and such fruits are characteristically seedless, not filled with numerous viable seeds. Therefore, the claim that parthenocarpic fruits contain numerous viable seeds is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Exactly two of the three claims—those regarding perisperm in black pepper and beet and false fruits like apple, strawberry, and cashew—are correct, while the claim about seediness in parthenocarpic fruits is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER2_MCQ_Q15 - Apomixis, polyembryony, and significance in hybrid agriculture

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding apomixis and polyembryony:

Statement I: Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction by producing seeds without fertilisation, as seen in some species of Asteraceae and grasses.

Statement II: In many Citrus and Mango varieties, some nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac, and develop into embryos, resulting in polyembryony.

Statement III: Converting hybrid crop varieties into apomicts would cause characters in the hybrid progeny to segregate, forcing farmers to buy hybrid seeds every year.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apomixis and polyembryony are specialised reproductive mechanisms in angiosperms with major significance in horticulture and the hybrid seed industry.

Step 2: Evaluation of Apomixis
A few flowering plants, such as some species of Asteraceae and grasses, produce seeds without fertilisation through apomixis. Because seeds are formed without gametic fusion, apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Nucellar Polyembryony
In many Citrus and Mango varieties, nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac, and develop into embryos. Consequently, each ovule contains more than one embryo, a phenomenon known as polyembryony. Thus, this claim is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Apomixis in Hybrid Crops
Normally, seeds collected from sexual hybrids segregate in the progeny and lose hybrid characters, forcing farmers to purchase costly hybrid seeds every year. If hybrids are made into apomicts, there is no segregation of characters in the hybrid progeny, allowing farmers to reuse their own hybrid seeds year after year. Claiming that apomixis would cause segregation is therefore the opposite of reality and incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims defining apomixis and nucellar polyembryony in Citrus and Mango are correct, whereas the claim that apomixis causes segregation in hybrid progeny is incorrect.
